Most research in the area of intrusion detection requires datasets to develop, evaluate or compare systems in
one way or another. In this ﬁeld, however, ﬁnding suitable datasets is a challenge on to itself. Most publicly
available datasets have negative qualities that limit their usefulness. In this article, we propose ID2T (Intrusion
Detection Dataset Toolkit) to tackle this problem. ID2T facilitates the creation of labeled datasets by injecting
synthetic atacks into background traﬃc. Te injected synthetic atacks blend themselves with the background
traﬃc by mimicking the background traﬃc’s properties to eliminate any trace of ID2T’s usage.
Tis work has three core contribution areas. First, we present a comprehensive survey on intrusion detection
datasets. In the survey, we propose a classiﬁcation to group the negative qualities we found in the datasets.
Second, the architecture of ID2T is revised, improved and expanded. Te architectural changes enable ID2T
to inject recent and advanced atacks such as the widespread EternalBlue exploit or botnet communication
paterns. Te toolkit’s new functionality provides a set of tests, known as TIDED (Testing Intrusion Detection
Datasets), that help identify potential defects in the background traﬃc into which atacks are injected. Tird,
we illustrate how ID2T is used in diﬀerent use-case scenarios to evaluate the performance of anomaly and
signature-based intrusion detection systems in a reproducible manner. ID2T is open source sofware and is
made available to the community to expand its arsenal of atacks and capabilities.

INTRODUCTION

a crucial task in today’s Internet age [36]. It is not only due to our dependency on the Internet,
but also because of the Internet’s threat landscape that NIDSs have become an almost mandatory
line of defense against atacks. Tis need to develop NIDSs that can keep up with evolving atacks
and motivated adversaries has yielded much research in the direction of identifying old and new,
previously unobserved, threats. Evaluating NIDS has intrinsic complexities and challenges that
need to be addressed irrespective of which intrusion detection method they use. Te evaluation of

NIDSs relies on quality datasets to assess their capabilities. Qality datasets are also what enables
accurate comparison of diﬀerent intrusion detection methods. Reliable datasets, however, are not
readily available.
Reliable datasets useful for the evaluation of NIDSs are hard to obtain. Widely available datasets
tend to be outdated, ofen lack labeled atacks and usually contain overlooked defects. Furthermore,
these datasets are ofen not publicly available or diﬃcult to obtain [18]. Most datasets are distributed
as PCAP (Packet Capture) ﬁles. Tese ﬁles, being in essence just an ordered collection of network
packets, can be thought as of having packets originating from one of two sources: a benign or a
malicious one. Packets originating from benign sources compose the normal or background traﬃc
of the dataset. Packets created by malicious activities on a network compose the atack traﬃc of
the dataset. To overcome the seemingly inherent diﬃculties of creating and sharing datasets, we
have developed ID2T. ID2T is a tool that creates and injects synthetic atack traﬃc into background
traﬃc. Rather that just na¨ıvely merging together the background and atack traﬃc, ID2T atempts
to replicate the properties of the background traﬃc in the synthetic atack traﬃc. Te level by
which properties are replicated is controlled by the user to suite their needs.
Users of ID2T are not conﬁned to only injecting the set of atacks provided. Te instruments to
develop new atacks are provided. Tese come in the form of an API (Application Programming
Interface) to easily extract, compare and replicate traﬃc properties.
Te design philosophy of ID2T is simple: background traﬃc is provided by the user and ID2T
adds atacks to the background traﬃc following the speciﬁcations of the user. Te injected atacks
are labeled and clearly identiﬁed for intrusion detection mechanisms to use; for instance, for
evaluation purposes. Figure 1 shows the main architectural components that together interact to
create datasets with synthetic atacks that replicate background traﬃc’s properties. Te inputs
of ID2T are a PCAP ﬁle containing background data and user supplied parameters. Its output is
a PCAP ﬁle injected with synthetic atacks, a labels ﬁle specifying the time and location of the
injected atacks, and a report on the statistical analysis of the background traﬃc.

1.2
The Limitations of ID2T
ID2T limits itself to replicating the properties of user-supplied background traﬃc into synthetically
generated atack traﬃc. Many atack scenarios are not aﬀected by this limitation, others, however,
may be negatively aﬀected. If an atack is not expected to alter the state of a network, the replication
strategy employed by ID2T is suﬃcient. In this category of atacks we ﬁnd most exploit atempts
and network reconnaissance scans. In contrast, if an atack is expected to change how packets are
produced and distributed in a network, ID2T will only approximate the real eﬀects of the atack.
Most denial of service and botnet atacks fall into this category.
A second limitation exists that is related to the labeling of atack traﬃc. A dataset suitable for
evaluating NIDS needs to have labeled atacks. ID2T indeed labels all synthetically injected atacks.
However, if the provided background traﬃc contains atacks, not all atacks would be labeled. To
try and leverage this problem, ID2T analyses the background traﬃc provided by the user so as to
highlight or make existing atacks stand out.
1.3
Outline
Te remainder of this article is structured as follows. In Section 2, we propose a set of requirements
for datasets that are suitable for the evaluation of NIDSs as well as for injecting synthetic atacks.
Section 3 discusses the state of the art in static and dynamic datasets for the evaluation of NIDS
and algorithms. We further categorize some of the defects found in these datasets. With Section 4
we begin the analysis of our toolkit (ID2T), its architecture and components. In addition, Section
5 touches one important component of ID2T that is responsible for the testing and analysis of
intrusion detection datasets. Subsequently, the atacks that can be generated by our toolkit are
presented in Section 6. Section 7, shows use cases that demonstrate how ID2T can be applied to
evaluate anomaly and signature-based NIDSs. Finally, Section 8 concludes this article.

REQUIREMENTS
Many requirements concern the creation and injection of synthetic atacks. On the one hand,
there are requirements related to the tool that injects the atacks. On the other hand, there are
requirements inherent to the resulting datasets, containing injected atacks, that are meant to
be used for the evaluation of IDSs (Intrusion Detection Systems). Tis section emphasizes this
distinction and divides the requirements into functional and non-functional ones.

2.1
Requirements of Datasets Suitable for the Evaluation of IDSs
Irrespective of whether datasets contain synthetic or real data, they need to conform to certain
requirements if they are to be used for the evaluation of NIDSs. From observations made in our
research in the ﬁeld of IDS (i.e., [7, 34–37]), as well as from the research of others [3, 18, 22, 29], we
have derived diﬀerent requirements that make datasets usable in the context of evaluating NIDSs.
In the following, these requirements are split into functional and non-functional ones.
2.1.1
Functional Requirements. Tese functional requirements focus on what is needed to con-
struct or assemble datasets that enable diﬀerent NIDSs to compare their performance against each
other.
(1) Payload availability — Due to privacy, network payloads are ofen unavailable. Tis limits
the capability of NIDSs to detect atacks at the payload level (e,g., application layer exploits).
To serve NIDSs that aim at detecting atacks at the payload level, one needs datasets that
include payloads.
(2) Labeled atacks — Datasets need labels that distinguish malicious from benign network
traﬃc. Labels enable NIDSs to determine their detection accuracy and to establish a direct
comparison against other NIDSs.
(3) Ground truth — Labeled traﬃc is not enough if it cannot be guaranteed that the background
traﬃc does not contain unlabeled atacks. Without ground truth, a direct comparison
between diﬀerent NIDSs is not possible.
(4) Growing — A growing dataset is one that is constantly updated with traces of recent
network traﬃc paterns and atacks.
(5) Atack diversity — Datasets usually focus on certain types of atacks. A dataset suitable for
the evaluation of diﬀerent NIDSs requires a diversiﬁed set of network atacks, from DoSs
(Denial of Services) to remote exploitation atempts.
2.1.2
Non-Functional Requirements. Te following non-functional requirements specify the
criteria datasets need to satisfy to be of practical use.
(1) Public availability or ease of reproducibility — Although being obvious, this requirement
needs to be explicitly stated. Datasets need to be created with the goal of becoming public or
easily reproduced. If a dataset is used for multiple evaluations, for the purpose of replicating
experiments, it must be made public. If privacy is a concern, anonymizing the data should
be carried out carefully so as to not introduce artifacts (see Section 3.3 for a deﬁnition of
the term). If the dataset cannot be public, reproducing it must be possible.
(2) Interoperability — Network data needs to be shared using a common format. Although not
a standard, the most commonly used format is the PCAP ﬁle format.
(3) Good quality — Trough our empirical experience of generating synthetic atacks, as well
as through the analysis of related work (see Section 3), we have identiﬁed diverse quality
issues that need to be taken into account when synthetic atacks are injected into real
traﬃc. Tese quality issues need to be addressed one by one, each one requiring special
atention. In Section 3, we further discuss these issues (termed artifacts) and categorize all
observations of these in other datasets.
2.2
Requirements for Injecting Synthetic Atacks
Tools for injecting synthetic atacks need to be built with the goal of crating useful datasets for
the evaluation of IDSs. Tese tools must be capable of working with arbitrary PCAP ﬁles; the
de facto standard for recording and sharing network communications. Tere should be no hard
assumptions regarding the provenance of these ﬁles nor how they are generated. It is for this

2.2.1
Functional Requirements. Te following functional requirements have been derived from
observations of how datasets are manually created. To alleviate the manual task of creating tailor-
made labeled datasets with atacks, a tool that injects atacks needs to take several functional
requirements into account. Tese next requirements focus on conferring tools with the ability to
customize already existing atacks and create new ones without much additional eﬀort.
(1) Packet level injection — In order to evaluate any type of network IDS, atacks must be
injected at the lowest common denominator that all network IDSs can use, i.e., packets.
Many IDSs directly use packets to perform intrusion detection. Tere is, however, another
family of IDSs that work on higher abstraction levels, such as network ﬂows [3]. If atacks
are injected at the packet level, both types of IDSs can beneﬁt from the generated datasets.
(2) Qerying interface for network properties — In order the generate realistic-looking syn-
thetic atacks, an input PCAP ﬁle needs to be analyzed to extract properties. Tese properties
amount to quantitative characteristics such as average used bandwidth per host, total number
of packets sent by a speciﬁc host, or the open ports observed for a given subnetwork. Tese
properties need to be made available to users that wish to inject atacks as well as to the
program that creates the synthetic atacks. An API is required to directly query the input
ﬁles into which atacks will be injected. Tis enables, for example, a synthetic port scan to
determine which ports, for a given host, were open in the input PCAP ﬁle.
(3) Atack diversity — Many network atack classiﬁcations exist. Tese classiﬁcations should
be taken into account when providing tools for generating and injecting synthetic atacks.
Rather than only focusing on a single type of atack, creating a diverse set of atacks is
required.
(4) Applicability to arbitrary PCAP ﬁles — As long as a PCAP ﬁle contains network traﬃc
alone, the ﬁle should be suitable for injecting synthetic atacks. To achieve this requirement,
PCAP ﬁles need to be analyzed to replicate their properties onto injected atacks. For
instance, if a network only contains local traﬃc (from the 192.168.1.0 subnet), by default
atacks should not originate from IP addresses outside this subnet (unless this is desired
and manually conﬁgured).
(5) Headless operation — Working with arbitrary PCAP ﬁles implies that their size is unbounded.
Packet captures of crowded networks can easily reach a size of hundreds of gigabytes.
Analyzing and injecting atacks into these ﬁles might take considerable time and memory
resources. It is assumed, therefore, that cluster environments or headless systems are used
to process large ﬁles. For this reason, tools that inject atacks need to work in headless
environments with small or no user interaction.
(6) Modeling of packet behavior and payload — Atack injection tools need to model atacks at
the packet and payload levels. Atacks at the packet level are more concerned about the
quantity of the sent packets rather than on the payload. Port scans and DDoS (Distributed
Denial of Service) atacks are examples of these. In contrast, atacks at the payload level
may carefully craf the data sent by each packet. Exploit atacks against a web server are
examples of these. Some atacks are concerned with both levels, such as when creating
synthetic botnet generated traﬃc. Tis traﬃc sometimes contains important payload
information that deﬁnes the atack, other times, the traﬃc is used as a DDoS atack in
which the payload is not important.

2.2.2
Non-Functional Requirements. Te following non-functional requirements are needed to
enable synthetic atack injection tools to process arbitrary PCAP ﬁles. Te main challenge when
not being limited to certain PCAP ﬁles is to consider the diﬀerent scenarios from where these
ﬁles may originate. Home and oﬃce environments generate limited traﬃc belonging to only few
sub-networks. In contrast, large enterprise or university networks may generate massive quantities
of data with heterogeneous characteristics.
(1) Scalability — When mimicking the properties of network data onto a synthetic atack, many
diﬀerent statistics need to be collected. Calculating statistics on top of network data is
typically demanding both in terms of memory and processing resources. Tools that inject
synthetic atacks need to take this into account and calculate statistics as eﬃciently as
possible. Tis guarantees the scalability of the tool when large PCAP ﬁles are analyzed and
injected with synthetic atacks.
(2) Extensibility — New atacks are developed each day. A set of tools and libraries are needed
to easily and rapidly model these new atacks for injection.
(3) Usability — One of the main reasons static datasets are widely used is due to their ease of use.
Static datasets have many disadvantages: they never change and become easily outdated.
Teir advantages, however, outweigh the disadvantages: they can be used immediately
without extensive setup. Tools that generate either real or synthetic traﬃc ofen require
complicated hardware and setups. To be as useful as static datasets, tools that inject
synthetic atacks need to be usable. Te user should be involved as litle as possible in the
injection process but have a detailed control over the injections.
(4) Open source and public availability — Researchers ofen build custom tools to evaluate
their work without making the tools available in open platforms. It is also common that
tools are lost when researchers change subject areas or institutions. For example, the tools
proposed by Shiravi et al. [29] and Brauckhoﬀet al. [4] can no longer be easily found online
although they used to be available.

RELATED WORK AND DEFECT ANALYSIS
A good quality dataset is one that allows researchers to identify the ability of an IDS to detect
anomalies [3], preferably allowing to draw valid conclusions about the appropriateness of the IDS
(its eﬃciency, accuracy, validity scope, etc). Although many of the available datasets nowadays
are valuable to the research community, they unfortunately fail to fulﬁll all the requirements
proposed in Section 2. Te existing datasets can be classiﬁed into two categories: static datasets
and dynamically generated datasets (see Figure 2 for a historical overview). In this section, ﬁrst, we
provide basic information about some of the most popular static datasets. Aferwards, we present a
description about the dynamically generated datasets. Lastly, this section discusses the deﬁciencies
and artifacts that can be found in datasets.
3.1
Static Datasets
A static dataset is a dataset that was generated once during a limited period of time. Such a dataset
can be collected from a real-world network or it can be generated synthetically. Currently, there
are several static datasets available for IDS evaluation purposes. Unfortunately, research suggests
that these datasets are not adequate for mainly two reasons. First, many of them are out of date.
Tey were created many years ago based on old versions of protocols, old applications, and atacks
that exploit old vulnerabilities. Tus, these datasets are not realistic datasets at the present time.
Second, these datasets contain many defects that indicate synthetic generation. In the following, we
brieﬂy discuss some well-known static datasets. It is worth to mention that similar datasets can be

3.1.1
DARPA 99. Te DARPA 99 is one of the most well-known datasets in the ﬁeld. In fact,
DARPA 99 is an upgraded version of the DARPA 98 dataset. Te two datasets were collected during
two intrusion detection evaluations [9, 20]. A testbed was developed to generate normal and
malicious traﬃc. Te normal traﬃc tended to be similar to that seen between a military base and
the Internet. A custom sofware automaton was used to simulate hundreds of users running UNIX
applications. In DARPA 98, the included atacks cover four categories, namely, DoS, R2L (Remote to
Local), U2R (User to Root), and Surveillance/Probing. Te traﬃc was collected for seven weeks
with labeled atacks and two weeks with unlabeled atacks. In DARPA 99, Windows NT hosts were
included in the evaluation as victims and more atacks types were covered. Te dataset consists of
two weeks of normal traﬃc with no atacks, one week with a few labeled atacks, and two weeks
of unlabeled traﬃc. DARPA 98 −99 datasets were highly innovative for their time and had been
widely used for IDS evaluation. However, later on, several studies have marked these datasets as
unreliable due to a number of limitations and issues (see Section 3.3).

was used heavily to evaluate IDSs at that time. Later on, several shortcomings in this dataset were
pointed out by various studies.

3.2
Dynamically Generated Datasets
Network behavior and traﬃc paterns change continuously and atacks evolve rapidly. Tis created
a need for datasets that are modiﬁable, extensible, and reproducible. Terefore, researchers have
proposed tools that are capable of generating synthetic datasets dynamically. Te main idea of
these tools is to consider the contemporary traﬃc characteristics and replicate them in synthetic
traﬃc, which in turn emphasizes the realism of the generated datasets. In this section, we present
the two existing dynamic datasets, followed by a brief comparison of them in Table 2.

there are almost two years of diﬀerence between them. We argue that in the last two years the

without creating an updated dataset from scratch. Te process of creating new synthetic atacks
that ID2T can inject is considerably faster than publishing new datasets every time a novel atack
or network conﬁguration needs to be tested.
In the second use case scenario, we use ID2T to test two popular NIDS. ID2T is a tool that enabled
the creation of network traﬃc that contained certain atacks that are easy to detect using the right
signatures. We showed how a properly conﬁgured installation of the Bro and Suricata NIDSs are
able to detect expected atacks. ID2T can be used, therefore, to verify the correct operation of
already deployed systems.
8
CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
We developed ID2T to try to address the long standing issue of not having reliable and reproducible
datasets in the NIDSs community. To evaluate systems, researchers in this community have a
tendency of using old, incomplete or private datasets that hamper their results. For example, it
is a common occurrence to ﬁnd new publications that use outdated datasets (such as the DARPA
1999 dataset). A system that demonstrates its capabilities on 19 year old network traﬃc cannot be
trusted to work on modern traﬃc. Te problem of acquiring reliable datasets lies in the diﬃculty
of creating datasets that are useful and, at the same time, fulﬁll the conditions or constraints of
the dataset’s creators. Privacy, for example, is a major concern that ends up impacting a dataset
because of the way data is anonymized or concealed.
With ID2T, we provide a tool that enables the creation of custom datasets while solving the
problems of reproducibility and privacy preservation. Instead of providing a single static dataset,
ID2T gives researchers the tools to inject synthetic atacks into background traﬃc they provide. Te
injected atacks replicate the characteristics of the background traﬃc to erase any trace that points
towards the usage of ID2T and the existence of synthetic traﬃc. With such a tool, we envision
researchers demonstrating the usage of their systems by specifying the type of background traﬃc
used and the parameters used to create an atack. For example, as illustrated in our use-case section
(see Section 7.1), we use backbone network traﬃc to detect DDoS atacks and SMB probing scans.

One key functionality of ID2T is that of replicating the characteristics of the provided background
traﬃc in the synthetic atacks it generates. Terefore, the properties of the background traﬃc
impact the injected atacks. We developed the TIDED module of ID2T (see Section 5) for the
purpose of helping researchers to determine if the characteristics of the provided background traﬃc
conform to their expectations. With such tests, for example, it is possible to determine if traﬃc
that claims to come from a backbone network reﬂects the properties of such a large network. With
TIDED, it is also possible to detect potential sources of defects that a dataset may have.
In future work, we wish to expand the capabilities of ID2T in two directions. First, we plan to
enlarge the arsenal of injectable atacks to include recent popular atacks. Second, we would like to
address the main limitation of ID2T. As it stands, ID2T has the limitation of not having a feedback
loop between the generated atacks and the background traﬃc. In real scenarios, an atack aﬀects
the characteristics of the network onto which it was launched. A DDoS atack, for example, may
cause a high number of TCP re-transmissions and lower average packet window sizes. Te atacks
generated by ID2T are limited to only replicating what is observed in the background traﬃc. It
is also desirable, for the purpose of creating more realistic traﬃc, to model the interaction that
an atack has on the background data. With such an interaction, atacks would also modify the
background traﬃc to either add, modify or delete packets.
